News global nation business lifestyle entertainment technology sports opinion LATEST NEWS STORIES HEADLINES METRO REGIONS NATION WORLD CDN NEWSLETTER www / West Philippine Sea West Philippine Sea 2012 Scarborough standoff spurred shift in PH military buildup By: Kurt Dela Peña - Content Researcher Writer / @inquirerdotnet INQUIRER.net / 02:53 PM November 27, 2026 Share: MANILA, Philippines — The 2012 maritime standoff with China at Scarborough Shoal marked the beginning of a “clear shift” in the Philippines’ military hardware acquisitions, an analyst said.
Dr. Alicor Panao, Inquirer data scientist and associate professor at the University of the Philippines, pointed this out as the Philippines’ moves to acquire US-made kinetic weaponry prompted speculation that the country might be preparing for something big.
Citing data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), Panao said the Philippines had been steadily acquiring military hardware for decades. What appears to have evolved over time, however, was not the decision to arm up but the composition of its acquisitions.
Between 1950 and 1989, utility transport, patrol craft and conventional guns accounted for 61.1% of the Philippines’ arms acquisition volume. Heavy combat platforms and armor represented another 31.4%, while precision missiles, sensors and drones made up just 7.6%.
This procurement mix remained largely unchanged between 1990 and 2013. Utility equipment still accounted for 58.8% of acquisitions, followed by heavy combat platforms at 37.7%.
Precision weapons and surveillance technologies represented only 3.4%, reflecting a force primarily equipped for internal security and basic mobility.
A clear shift emerged beginning in 2014, following the 2012 maritime standoff with China at Scarborough Shoal, which exposed the Philippines’ lack of external defense capabilities.
“It set an inflection point for the Revised AFP Modernization Program enacted under President Benigno Aquino III, which laid the legal, budgetary, and multi-horizon framework for rebuilding external territorial defense,” he said.

From 2014 to 2025, precision missiles, sensors and drones accounted for 53.7% of total acquisition volume, exceeding the combined shares of heavy combat platforms, at 25.1%, and utility equipment, at 21.2%.
During this period, the Philippines also diversified its suppliers, acquiring transport aircraft, helicopters and sonars from the United States while sourcing air defense systems, missiles and naval platforms from partners such as Israel, South Korea, India and France, Panao said.
“This trajectory continued during the Duterte administration, despite its supposed conciliatory rhetoric and perceived diplomatic pivot toward China,” he said.
Based on SIPRI arms-transfer records from 1950 to 2025, the Duterte administration appears to have facilitated the largest cumulative arms procurement volume of any Philippine presidency, recording 2,192.95 in SIPRI trend-indicator volume between 2016 and 2021.
Of this volume, 75.5% was dedicated to precision missiles, sensors and drones.
“This suggests that the direction of defense modernization was not simply a reflection of the foreign policy preferences of individual presidents and has held steady across multiple presidencies,” he said.
